atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 was a 51-year-old female in Spain with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included cirrhosis, stable CKD, obesity, 25-hydroxyvitamin D use, and Caucasian ethnicity. Time to onset was 4 months; biopsy proven; X-ray and CT showed upper-lung calcification and mammography showed bilateral vascular-pattern calcifications. Before teriparatide SCr 1.33 mg/dL, GFR 45.1 mL/min/1.73 m2, corrected calcium 10.1 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.6 mg/dL, calcium-phosphorus product 36 mg2/dL2; at 4 months SCr 1.57, GFR 37.1, corrected calcium 10.8, phosphorus 3.9, calcium-phosphorus product 42, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 84 ng/mL. Management: teriparatide and vitamin D were discontinued; IV pamidronate was followed by prolonged IV sodium thiosulfate and IV ibandronate. Outcome: improved.

Case 2 was a 84-year-old female in Israel with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included COPD, diabetes, warfarin, and intermittent unspecified oral steroids. Time to onset was 6 months; biopsy not reported and imaging not reported. Baseline calcium and phosphorus were reported within normal limits; actual values were not reported. Management: teriparatide was discontinued; plastic surgery included skin grafting and tendon extension. Outcome: improved.

Case 3 was a 82-year-old female in USA with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included peripheral vascular occlusive disease, an unspecified corticosteroid, and warfarin. Time to onset was 3 months; biopsy proven; imaging not reported. Relevant laboratory values were not reported. Management: teriparatide was discontinued and wound care was provided. Outcome: not resolved.

Case 4 was a 86-year-old female in USA with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included polymyalgia rheumatica, calcium supplementation, chronic prednisone, chronic warfarin, and Caucasian ethnicity. Time to onset was 2 months; biopsy proven; imaging not reported. SCr 1.1 mg/dL, GFR 46 mL/min/1.73 m2, uncorrected calcium 9.4 mg/dL, ionized calcium 5.4 mg/dL, and phosphorus 3.5 mg/dL. Management: teriparatide and warfarin were discontinued; aggressive wound care and zoledronic acid 3 months later were reported. Outcome: resolved despite reinitiation of warfarin.

Case 5 was a 66-year-old female in USA with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included obesity, rheumatoid arthritis, prednisone, and warfarin. Time to onset was 2 months; biopsy proven; imaging not reported. Renal function and calcium-phosphate product were reported as normal; actual values were not reported. Management: teriparatide and warfarin were discontinued and IV sodium thiosulfate was given; the patient later transitioned to hospice because of lesion progression and intractable pain. Outcome: death.

Case 6 was a 74-year-old female in Finland with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included rheumatism, prednisolone, warfarin, and calcium supplementation. Time to onset was 20 months; biopsy proven; imaging not reported. Relevant laboratory values were not reported. Management: teriparatide was discontinued and IV sodium thiosulfate was given. Outcome: improved.

Case 7 was a 86-year-old female in USA with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included calcium supplementation and chronic warfarin. Time to onset was a few weeks; a specific time-to-onset was not reported; biopsy proven; imaging not reported. SCr was 1.1 mg/dL. Management: not reported. Outcome: not reported.

Case 8 was a 67-year-old female in Finland with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included rheumatism, calcium supplementation, cortisone, and methylprednisolone. Time to onset was not reported; biopsy proven; imaging not reported. Ionized calcium, phosphorus, and creatinine were reported within normal reference ranges; actual values were not reported. Management: teriparatide was discontinued and sodium thiosulfate of unspecified route was given. Outcome: not resolved.

Case 9 was a 86-year-old female in USA with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included polymyalgia rheumatica or rheumatoid arthritis and warfarin. Time to onset was 2 months; biopsy proven; imaging not reported. Uncorrected calcium was 9.9 mg/dL, phosphorus was reported as normal, and the patient was reported not to be in renal failure. Management: teriparatide was discontinued only. Outcome: not resolved.

Case 10 was a 80-year-old female in Spain with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included obesity, polymyalgia rheumatica, and prednisone. Time to onset was 2 months; biopsy proven; imaging not reported. Renal function tests and calcium-phosphate product were reported as normal; actual values were not reported. Management: teriparatide was discontinued only. Outcome: improved.

Case 11 was a 81-year-old female in USA with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included Sjogren's syndrome, vascular blockage, and calcium supplementation. Time to onset was 9 months; biopsy proven; patient-reported CT of unspecified type was negative for cancer. No prior history of hypercalcemia was reported; after teriparatide initiation the patient reported having too much calcium in her blood, but the value was not reported. Management: teriparatide, calcium, and vitamin D were discontinued only. Outcome: not resolved.

Case 12 was a 47-year-old male in USA with calciphylaxis after teriparatide exposure. Reported risk factors included amyloidosis, stable CKD on dialysis for 25 years, calcitriol, fludrocortisone, and age. Time to onset was 1 month; biopsy-confirmed calciphylaxis was reported, but a conflicting statement said the biopsy looked like cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa. Relevant laboratory values were not reported. Management: teriparatide was discontinued only. Outcome: resolved.
In three cases with chronic warfarin use, the authors judged calciphylaxis onset to be more temporally associated with teriparatide initiation.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors considered the series different from typical uremic calciphylaxis because 10 of 12 cases occurred in patients without CKD and the two CKD cases were described as stable.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: our series included 10 of 12 cases of calciphylaxis following teriparatide exposure in non-uremic patients

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors considered teriparatide-associated calciphylaxis biologically plausible because teriparatide affects calcium and phosphorus homeostasis and may affect vascular calcification pathways.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The development of calciphylaxis following teriparatide exposure is biologically plausible.

atoms.canonical_statement: The spontaneous-report case series could not establish teriparatide as the sole cause of calciphylaxis relative to other underlying risk factors.

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 12 had diagnostic ambiguity because the table reported biopsy-confirmed calciphylaxis but also a conflicting biopsy description resembling cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa.
The authors concluded that teriparatide exposure combined with underlying risk factors may have triggered new-onset calciphylaxis in this mostly non-uremic case series.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors stated that teriparatide-associated calciphylaxis was most likely rare in the context of nearly 20 years of US marketing.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: calciphylaxis associated with teriparatide use is most likely a rare event

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors advised considering teriparatide-associated calciphylaxis in the differential diagnosis when patients develop new calciphylaxis or worsening existing disease.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: should be considered in a differential diagnosis among patients presenting with new-onset calciphylaxis or worsening of existing disease

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors emphasized prompt diagnosis and management because calciphylaxis can be life-threatening and earlier intervention may improve outcomes.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Expedited diagnosis and management by a clinician are important because calciphylaxis may be life-threatening
